title: Café
goal: Order lunch for you and your friend Ana. Ana is allergic to nuts.
twist: The dish Ana wants is sold out, and two of the alternatives contain nuts.
note: Fictional dialogue constructed for teaching purposes. The Harbour Café menu is fictional.

start.speaker: Narrator
start.line: You and your friend Ana are at the café counter. Read the menu board. You want the tomato soup. Ana wants the vegetable curry, and she is allergic to nuts.

greet.speaker: Priya
greet.line: Hi! What can I get you?

options.text: Could I have a tomato soup, please? And for my friend, the vegetable curry.
options.feedback: Polite and complete. You ordered for both of you in a natural way.

options.text: Soup. Curry.
options.feedback: Priya can guess, but one-word orders sound abrupt. Add 'Could I have ..., please?'
options.recast: Could I have a tomato soup and a vegetable curry, please?

options.text: I would like eat one soup tomato.
options.feedback: Two common errors: 'like to eat' (or just 'like'), and in English the describing word comes first: 'tomato soup'.
options.recast: I'd like a tomato soup, please.

abrupt.speaker: Priya
abrupt.line: Er, OK. One tomato soup. And is the curry for you too?

friendorder.speaker: Priya
friendorder.line: And what would your friend like?

options.text: And for my friend, the vegetable curry, please.
options.feedback: Clear. 'And for my friend, ...' tells Priya who the dish is for.

options.text: She eats curry.
options.feedback: Correct grammar, but it sounds like a fact about Ana's habits, not an order.
options.recast: She'd like the vegetable curry, please.

options.text: For my friend is the curry vegetable.
options.feedback: Say 'the vegetable curry' (describing word first) and leave out 'is'.
options.recast: For my friend, the vegetable curry.

soldout.speaker: Priya
soldout.line: Oh, I'm really sorry. We've run out of the vegetable curry. The pesto pasta and the Harbour salad are both really nice.
soldout.slower: Sorry, there is no more curry today. You can have the pasta or the salad.
soldout.spell: Pesto: P, E, S, T, O.

options.text: She's allergic to nuts. Does the pasta have any nuts in it?
options.feedback: Very important and well done. Always say the allergy first, then ask about the dish.

options.text: What's in the Harbour salad?
options.feedback: A good clarification question. It is also a good idea to say that Ana has an allergy.

options.text: OK, the pasta then.
options.feedback: Grammatical and polite, but risky: you didn't mention Ana's allergy. With allergies, always tell the staff.
options.recast: She's allergic to nuts. Is the pasta OK for her?

options.text: She is allergy of nuts.
options.feedback: Priya understands, luckily. The adjective is 'allergic', and it goes with 'to': 'allergic to nuts'.

pesto.speaker: Priya
pesto.line: Good question. The pesto has pine nuts in it, so that's no good. And the salad has walnuts.

salad.speaker: Priya
salad.line: It's leaves, tomato, cheese and walnuts. Is anyone allergic to anything?

allergy-recast.speaker: Priya
allergy-recast.line: Oh, she's allergic to nuts? Thanks for telling me. Then not the pesto or the salad. They both have nuts.

danger.speaker: Priya
danger.line: Just so you know, the pesto has pine nuts in it and the salad has walnuts. Does anyone have an allergy?
danger.slower: The pasta has nuts. The salad has nuts. Is anyone allergic?

options.text: Yes, she's allergic to nuts. Is there anything without nuts?
options.feedback: Good. You said the allergy clearly and asked for a safe choice.

options.text: It's fine. She can just eat around them.
options.feedback: This is a safety problem, not only a language problem. Don't guess with allergies; tell the staff and ask.
options.recast: Actually, she's allergic to nuts. What can she have?

options.text: Yes. She don't eat nuts.
options.feedback: Use 'doesn't' with 'she'. And 'allergic' is clearer than 'doesn't eat': it tells Priya it is a health issue.
options.recast: Yes. She doesn't eat nuts. She's allergic.

careful.speaker: Priya
careful.line: I'd really not risk it with an allergy. Let me find something without nuts.

alternative.speaker: Priya
alternative.line: For her, the tomato soup or the cheese sandwich are fine. They're both nut-free.
alternative.slower: She can have the soup or the cheese sandwich. They have no nuts.

build.prompt: Choose the cheese sandwich for Ana instead.

nearMisses.feedback: The pesto pasta has pine nuts. Choose a nut-free dish.
The pesto pasta has pine nuts. Choose a nut-free dish.
'I'll have' is for you. The sandwich is for Ana, so say 'She'll have'.
'I'll have' is for you. The sandwich is for Ana, so say 'She'll have'.

build.hint: Who is it for? Start with that person. Then the dish, then 'please'.

options.text: She'll have the cheese sandwich instead, please.
options.feedback: Clear decision. 'Instead' shows you changed the order.

options.text: Just give her anything.
options.feedback: It sounds careless, and Priya can't choose for Ana. Make a clear choice.
options.recast: She'll have the cheese sandwich, please.

options.text: She will to have the sandwich of cheese.
options.feedback: No 'to' after 'will'. And English says 'cheese sandwich', not 'sandwich of cheese'.

choose-for-her.speaker: Priya
choose-for-her.line: Hmm, I'd better not choose for her. The soup or the sandwich?

eatin.speaker: Priya
eatin.line: Lovely. Is that to eat in or take away?
eatin.slower: Will you eat here, or take the food with you?

options.text: To eat in, please.
options.feedback: Short and natural. This is the usual answer.

options.text: Why do you need to know?
options.feedback: Not wrong, but it sounds suspicious. This is a normal question in cafés.

options.text: For eat here.
options.feedback: Priya understands. The fixed phrase is 'to eat in' or 'to have here'.

explain.speaker: Priya
explain.line: Eat in means you sit here. Take away means you take the food with you. We use different plates and boxes.

options.text: Just two glasses of water, please. That's all, thanks.
options.feedback: Good. 'That's all, thanks' tells Priya you have finished ordering.

options.text: No. Nothing. Finish.
options.feedback: Three short words sound cold. 'No, that's all, thanks' is friendlier.

options.text: No, it's all, thank.
options.feedback: The fixed phrase is 'That's all, thanks' (or 'thank you').

total.speaker: Priya
total.line: So, one tomato soup and one cheese sandwich, to eat in. That's ten thirty, please. I'll tell the kitchen about the nut allergy.
total.slower: One soup and one cheese sandwich. Ten thirty, please. I will tell the kitchen about the allergy.

options.text: Great, thank you. Can I pay by card?
options.feedback: Friendly and practical. You thanked Priya and asked about payment.

options.text: Sorry, could you repeat the price?
options.feedback: Good repair. Prices and numbers are hard to catch.

options.text: Ten thirty? In my country it's much cheaper.
options.feedback: Grammatical, but comparing prices with your country can sound rude in a service encounter.
options.recast: Ten thirty. OK, can I pay by card?

options.text: Thank you, is very kind.
options.feedback: English needs a subject: 'That's very kind' or 'You're very kind'.

priceagain.speaker: Priya
priceagain.line: Of course. Ten thirty. Card is fine.

end.speaker: Narrator
end.line: Lunch is ordered. Ana has a safe, nut-free sandwich, and the kitchen knows about her allergy.
end.summary: Task complete: order placed for two, allergy explained, sold-out item replaced.
